ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a warm, informal academic-video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns during greetings and discussion, and long, highly structured monologues during presentations. Early conversation is loose and chatty, full of greetings, side remarks, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), and occasional technical-check interruptions. Speakers hedge frequently with “um,” “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” and self-corrections; there are many false starts, repetitions, and unfinished phrases, especially from non-native speakers. Questions are usually polite and prefaced with praise or disclaimers such as “great talk,” “quick question,” or “naive question,” then develop into multipart, exploratory prompts. Responses are generous and collaborative, often validating the question before answering, while disagreement or uncertainty is expressed indirectly through qualifications rather than blunt contradiction. Participants build on one another by referencing prior questions, adding related possibilities, and inviting follow-up collaboration. Formality rises for introductions and talks but remains conversational, with presenters using signposting, rhetorical questions, and repeated framing phrases to guide the audience.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - So what I keep coming back to, and this is just from the last couple of projects I've run, is that you pay for it later if you skip the pilot, you always do, and then...
  - Mm.
  - Sorry, can I ask- is that the same pilot as the spring one?
Opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating an AI math tutor used in middle-school classrooms and deciding what it should and should not do for students.

speakers.name: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a postdoctoral researcher in human-centered AI with six years of experience building and evaluating educational software. He maintains the tutor's event pipeline and works with trace logs, error analyses, offline model evaluation, and A/B tests of hint policies. His recent work has focused on whether structured prompt sequences help students complete multi-step algebra problems without exposing answer keys too quickly.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats the pilot as a system-evaluation problem: the team needs reliable event definitions, comparable interaction data, and clear policy rules for what the tutor does after a wrong answer, repeated hint request, or long pause. He is especially concerned that teacher observations alone will not establish whether a particular hint sequence improved performance. He tends to frame support in terms of the tutor's ordered prompts, branching logic, and measurable student responses.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
speakers.background: Dr. Alvarez is a postdoctoral researcher in mathematics education with eight years of classroom-based research experience across grades 6–8. She has conducted lesson observations, teacher interviews, video-supported discourse analysis, and formative-assessment studies in districts serving multilingual learners. Her work examines how teachers interpret student thinking and adjust instruction during problem solving.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Alvarez evaluates the tutor through its place in classroom instruction rather than as a stand-alone intervention. She wants to know whether its feedback gives teachers usable information, whether students remain responsible for explaining their reasoning, and whether support can be intentionally adjusted as learners become more independent. She views implementation fidelity as including teachers' decisions, classroom routines, and the quality of follow-up conversations, not merely whether students clicked through a sequence of screens.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Anika Patel
speakers.background: Dr. Patel is a fourth-year PhD student in educational psychology studying math anxiety, achievement motivation, and students' reactions to evaluative feedback. She has experience administering brief repeated surveys, conducting think-aloud interviews, and analyzing within-student changes in affect during computerized learning tasks. Her dissertation investigates how the wording and timing of corrective feedback affect persistence after mistakes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Patel focuses on the learner's emotional interpretation of the tutor: whether repeated hints feel encouraging or like evidence of failure, whether an answer reveal reduces distress at a useful moment or reinforces avoidance, and whether progress displays motivate students differently depending on prior confidence. She advocates pairing usage logs with short, low-burden measures of anxiety, perceived competence, and willingness to try another problem, while recognizing that conclusions from controlled psychology studies may not transfer neatly to ordinary classrooms.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Create a natural planning-meeting transcript involving Dr. Chen (computer science), Dr. Alvarez (education), and Dr. Patel (psychology). Dr. Chen and Dr. Alvarez must each use the term "scaffolding" and make their distinct meanings clear from the surrounding discussion, without explicitly announcing that they define it differently. Dr. Chen uses it to mean the tutor's structured sequence of algorithmic hint prompts and problem-solving supports. Dr. Alvarez uses it to mean temporary instructional support that teachers intentionally adjust and withdraw as students gain independence. Dr. Patel may contribute to discussion of anxiety and feedback but must not provide a third definition of scaffolding. The team should agree to log hint sequences and teacher interventions during the pilot, while leaving the exact criteria for when automated support is faded unresolved. Do not mention the benchmark, jargon detection, or the intended answer.

meanings.meaning: A structured, system-implemented sequence of algorithmic hints and problem-solving prompts that guides a student through a math problem.
Temporary instructional support, deliberately adjusted and withdrawn by a teacher as a learner develops independent competence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I know we're all coming from other things, so maybe today we can just get clear on what we want to notice during the six weeks—not just whether students get the equations right, but what the tutor leaves us able to see about their reasoning and the teacher follow-up. Um, Min-Jae, could you start by walking us through what teachers would actually see after class?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: After class, teachers would see a per-student timeline: each problem, submitted steps, wrong answers, hint requests, the exact hint sequence delivered, answer reveals, and whether the student later corrected the work. I would keep the summary view fairly simple, but the underlying events need to remain available; otherwise a completed equation can look like successful support when we cannot tell what actually preceded it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: That level of detail is useful. Could the teacher-facing view- could it make it easy to see the difference between a student who requested three hints and then made a meaningful revision, and one who more or less clicked through to an answer? I'm thinking teachers won't have time to reconstruct every timeline for all students.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: I can have the summary classify the trajectory instead of just counting hints. So, for example, it could show three hints followed by a new submitted step and eventual correction, versus three hints followed by an answer reveal or no response. I’d be careful about automatically calling a revision meaningful, though. The dashboard can surface the sequence, but the exact submitted steps should still be one click away.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: That distinction matters for persistence too. Min-Jae, can the event stream keep the time from an incorrect response to a hint, and then from the hint to the next attempt? I wouldn't treat a correction after several hints as equivalent if the student is just moving quickly toward an answer reveal rather than actually re-engaging.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: We can log both intervals precisely, and also whether the next event is a typed step, another hint request, an answer reveal, or just no activity. The hard part is interpreting a long gap. It might be reflection, but in a classroom it could also mean they're writing on paper or waiting for the teacher, so I'd keep it as a signal rather than label it frustration.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: And that ambiguity is exactly why I'd want a very brief in-the-moment check, rather than inferring affect from latency alone. Maybe after a small sampled set of feedback episodes, we'd ask one item about willingness to try another problem or perceived competence, not after every hint, obviously. We should first check whether the consent arrangement permits linking that to the event data with coded IDs.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: I think the sampled check is reasonable, but it should attach to a clearly defined episode in the log, say after a second or third hint, instead of a general time window. Otherwise we won't know which prompt sequence the response refers to. And Sofia, if a teacher has stepped in during that episode, even a minimal flag would matter a great deal for interpreting- for how we interpret it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: A minimal teacher flag would help, but I want to check with the teachers first. During active problem solving, even one extra marker can be a lot. And if we use hint level as a scaffolding measure, I’d be cautious. The log can show what was delivered, but it can’t by itself tell us whether that support was appropriately faded or whether the student could explain the step afterward.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: That makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: For the pilot, I'd treat scaffolding as the ordered sequence the system actually delivers, not just the highest hint level reached. Then we can test whether a sequence is followed by an independent next step or just completion. But Sofia's right, whether it was appropriately faded needs either a brief follow-up item or teacher context.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: A follow-up item should distinguish relief from readiness, if we can keep it to two taps, maybe “I understand what to try next” and “I want to try the next problem without help.” In my prior task data, those came apart, and I’d expect teacher presence and peers to make that separation even messier here.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: Okay, two taps.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: Two taps sounds plausible, especially if it comes after a defined episode. I’d still want a very small reasoning check somewhere, not necessarily on-screen every time, because a student can feel ready, complete the next item, and still not be able to say why they did the same operation on both sides. Maybe, maybe the teachers could choose a few students for a quick follow-up conversation each week?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: That could work, but I’d want the conversations tied to a specific item or episode and the coded student ID. Otherwise we get useful reasoning evidence, but we can’t tell if it followed the second-hint path, a reveal, or a teacher intervention. Could the teachers realistically just note the problem number for those conversations?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: Noting the problem number seems realistic if the conversation is already part of the teacher's normal circulation, but I wouldn't ask them to do it for every exchange. Maybe each teacher selects two or three students a week and records the item, plus a very short indication of what prompted the talk, like a reveal, repeated hinting, or their own observation. I need to ask them whether that even, um, fits their routines, though.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: That gives us enough structure to join the interview notes to the trace without making teachers annotate the whole lesson. I’d keep the prompt categories fixed, reveal, repeated hinting, or teacher observation, because otherwise we’ll end up with labels that can’t be compared across the three classes. The teacher can add a few words if they’re useful, but the coded item and category are the essential part.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: Fixed categories make sense for the trace. I’d just want to leave room for “teacher observation” to include, say, when the student’s explanation doesn’t match the completed work. That’s the kind of case I don’t want us to flatten into a successful correction. And I’ll ask the teachers whether two or three of those brief conferences a week—whether that feels workable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: I'd add one option to those categories, visible hesitation or withdrawal, if teachers feel they can recognize it without turning it into a diagnosis. That may be especially useful around repeated hints or reveals because a completed item can mask a student who is, is disengaging. But I agree we'd need the brief self-report to know what that behavior meant.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: I like that as an observation prompt, not as a claim about the student. Maybe the fixed list is reveal, repeated hinting, teacher observation, and visible hesitation or withdrawal, and teachers can mark more than one. Then in the short conference we can see whether what looked like withdrawal was confusion, waiting, or I lost the thread there, something else.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: Multiple categories is fine. The event record can store them as separate flags instead of forcing one explanation. I just would not use visible hesitation to trigger a different tutor policy during the pilot, since it isn't available to the system in real time and we'd, we'd confound the hint-sequence comparison.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: I agree, not as a live trigger. I’d just want the sampled two-item check to happen after some reveal episodes, as well as repeated-hint episodes. Otherwise we may only learn what students report when they stay in the hint path, not whether a reveal is functioning as relief or as- whether it’s avoidance.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: Yes, we need both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: And when we look at those reveal episodes, I’d want the teacher’s follow-up conversation to ask for an explanation, not just another correct answer. Otherwise we may count relief, readiness, and completion, but still miss whether the student can reconstruct the equation step on their own, and that’s...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: Yes. For those sampled reveal cases, the explanation prompt should be linked to the original item, and we should record whether the student supplies a new step versus repeats the displayed solution. That gives us a modest independence measure without treating the reveal itself as evidence that the support worked.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: And I’d make the prompt something like, “Show me what you would do next, and why,” instead of asking them to recite the displayed solution. That gives the teacher a small window into whether the reveal became a resource for reasoning or just an answer they copied. I’ll see whether the teachers can use that wording naturally in those brief conferences.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: Yes—asking for a new step gets closer to readiness than a confidence rating alone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: Yes—the item-level trace will make that explanation check interpretable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Alvarez
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should let everyone go a few minutes early. I’ll check with the teachers about what fits their routines, and we can pick this up next time. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Min-Jae Chen
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye, everyone.
